product.name: What you're building
product.system_prompt: This chat pins down the solution: what it actually does, the core mechanism that solves the problem, what belongs in a first version and what is explicitly out, and how the founder would know it is working. Push for concrete scope over vision. Keep it product-level — stack and integration details are memories, not brief features.

customer.name: The market
customer.system_prompt: This chat covers the market: the beachhead customer and their behaviour, roughly how many of them there are, where they already gather, and who else already serves them. Name real competitors and alternatives when you know them, then push hard on what makes this different. Rough sizing is fine — precision is not the point, direction is.

problem.name: The problem
problem.system_prompt: You are the founder's AI co-founder. This chat pins the core problem — who hurts, how badly, and why now. Push past vague statements to something concrete. When you have enough, propose a crisp one-sentence problem for the brief and ask them to confirm.

replies.text:
Here's a first pass — tell me where it's off.

Problem: group camping trips have no single source of truth, so one person ends up chasing gear lists, food assignments, and logistics through scattered texts and a spreadsheet nobody updates.

Who hurts: the informal trip organizer — the friend who always ends up planning — burns hours nagging people and still risks arriving with duplicate gear or missing something critical.

Cost: their time, plus the stress of being the bottleneck everyone blames if something goes wrong on the trip.

The part I'm least sure about — is this really the organizer's pain alone, or does the whole group feel the coordination mess (duplicate gear, confusion about who's bringing what)?

Good — so it's shared pain, not just the organizer's. That reframes who this is for.

Before I lock the problem statement: how does the group cope with this mess today — is it really just texts and a shared spreadsheet, or something messier?

Locking that in — the mess lives in texts and a shared spreadsheet that nobody keeps current, and everyone feels it, not just the organizer.

One thing left before I nail the problem statement: what does this actually cost the group — wasted money on duplicate gear, wasted time re-confirming things, or real risk if something critical gets missed?
Let me make that concrete — when the coordination breaks down, what actually happens on the trip?

Good to know it's not rare — this bites on every single trip, big or small.

So when it does hit, what's the actual damage: money wasted on duplicate gear, hours wasted re-confirming who's bringing what, or real risk — like showing up without something critical?

That's the full shape of it, then: duplicate gear wastes money, re-confirming wastes hours, and missing something critical creates real risk — and it happens every trip.

Here's my crisp version: "Group camping trips lack a single source of truth, so the whole group — not just the organizer — pays in wasted money on duplicate gear, wasted time re-confirming logistics, and real risk when something critical gets missed, every single trip."

Does that capture it, or is one piece over/under-weighted?

Locked in, then — that's the problem statement.

Last piece for this chat: why hasn't something like a shared spreadsheet or app already fixed this? What makes people stick with texts and stale spreadsheets instead?

That paints the real picture — it's not just a stale spreadsheet, it's texts piling up, phone calls to chase people down, actual arguments, and something still slipping through anyway. That's basically the answer to why nothing's fixed this: the tools people use (texts, calls, spreadsheets) don't hold anyone accountable, so the gaps repeat every time.

That locks the problem side for this chat — organizer plans, group suffers, no single source of truth, every trip, from day one.

That fairness thread matters — it's not just wasted time, it's often one person fronting money and then having to chase everyone else to get paid back. Here's the sharpened problem statement:

Group camping trips lack a single source of truth, so the whole group — not just the organizer — pays in wasted money on duplicate gear, wasted time re-confirming logistics, unfair money burdens on whoever fronts costs, and real risk when something critical gets missed, every single trip, from day one.

Does that get the whole picture now?

That's a strong root cause — nobody's built a tool that actually replaces texts, calls, and spreadsheets, so groups just default to what's familiar even though it keeps causing fights and gaps.

The onboarding idea is sharp too: AI asks the host a few questions, auto-builds a shared board of what's needed, people claim items, and everyone gets an email recap of what they're bringing. That's a real feature, not just a nice-to-have.

With the problem locked and a feature taking shape, the last open piece is the core value — once this exists, what's the one thing people feel that they don't feel today: fairness, peace of mind, or just saved time?

Here's a first pass:

Watering holes - where organizers already hang:
1. r/CampingandHiking and r/Ultralight (Reddit)
2. Local hiking/camping Facebook groups and Meetup backpacking groups
3. REI Co-op event boards and outdoor gear shop community pages

First move this week: post in one of those groups asking organizers how they currently split gear and costs, then offer a simple demo link to whoever responds - that's your first real signal.

Now the piece I need most: what's the core value in one line - the thing that makes an organizer say "finally"?
1. No one gets stuck holding the bag (money fairness)
2. Nothing gets forgotten (safety/completeness)
3. Everyone knows what to bring, automatically (coordination ease)
4. Help me decide

First pass:

Beachhead: recurring friend or family groups (roughly 4-10 people) who camp together 2+ times a year — not solo campers or one-off bachelor parties, since they don't feel the repeated pain enough to switch tools.

Size (rough): tens of millions of Americans camp yearly, and a meaningful slice of those go in recurring groups — likely low millions of "organizer + regular crew" units in the US alone.

Who else serves them: Splitwise (splits money after the fact, no gear/checklist), Notion/Trello templates (DIY, no automation), and the group text + spreadsheet combo you've already flagged. Nobody's built a camping-specific coordination tool yet.

Sharpest question: what makes a group actually switch from their free spreadsheet — is it that the AI onboarding kills the setup effort, or that it fixes the money fairness problem no spreadsheet solves?

Here's a first pass — tell me where I'm wrong.

Core mechanism: the host answers a few AI-guided onboarding questions about the trip, and that auto-generates a shared checklist/board. Group members claim items they're bringing, and everyone gets an email recap of what they committed to.

V1 includes:
1. AI onboarding for the host
2. Auto-generated shared checklist/board
3. Claiming items as a group member
4. Email recap of claimed items

Out of v1:
1. Money tracking or expense splitting
2. In-app chat or messaging
3. Native mobile app

The thing I'm least sure about: the problem you described includes unfair money burdens, but my v1 draft only handles gear and logistics, not who owes what. Should v1 touch money at all, or stay pure logistics for now?

Before locking a name, worth naming the feel it should have — that steers everything else. Here are three directions, each with a different personality:

1. Campfire Tab — the shared tab that keeps every camping trip fair (warm, friendly)

2. TrailSplit — split camping costs and gear fairly, automatically (practical, trustworthy)

3. BasePlan — the one shared plan for your whole camping crew (clean, organized, a bit premium)

Which feel is closest to what you want people to feel when they open it?

Good question — for a group trip tool, these feel like the natural lanes to pick from:

1. Trustworthy — like it's got your back, nothing gets missed or forgotten

2. Playful — fun, low-stakes, matches the vibe of planning a trip with friends

3. Premium — polished, organized, feels like a step up from texts and spreadsheets

Which one matches how you want it to feel?

Warm and communal — got it, that's a good fit for a group trip tool. That points toward names like Campfire Tab or Basecamp-style names over something clinical like TrailSplit.

Should I lean into that direction for the name options, or do you want to see a wider mix first?

Warm and communal, staying away from anything clinical — here's another round in that direction:

1. Basecamp Tab — the shared home base for your trip's gear and costs

2. Trailmates — the tool that keeps your camping crew on the same page

3. Campfire Ledger — a friendly shared tally of who's bringing and paying what

4. Groundwork — the plan your whole group builds together before the trip

Any of these closer, or still not it?

Here's a first pass:

Who pays: most likely the whole group, not just the organizer — since they're the ones splitting costs already, a small per-trip fee spread across members feels fairer than dumping it on whoever organizes.

Shape: probably freemium — free to create a basic board and claim items, paid to unlock the AI onboarding and email recaps (the parts that save the most time).

Price: something like $2-4 per person per trip, or a flat $15-25 per trip the group splits.

Does charging the group per trip feel right, or should the organizer be the one who pays instead?

Got it — so paying to join isn't just revenue, it's the commitment mechanism: if you've paid, you're locked in and less likely to flake or under-communicate. That's a nice double duty for the price point.

What should be free before that payment kicks in — can people see the board and claim items before paying, or does payment gate entry to the trip entirely?
Let me put it simply: right now do people need to pay before they can even see the shared board, or can they look around and claim items for free — and only pay once they're committed to going?

So it's flat — everyone pays the same $1-5, whether they're starting the trip or joining it. That answers what they pay; now I still want to know what's visible for free.

Can someone see the board and what's needed before they pay, or does payment happen first before they see anything?
